newsitem.title: IRAN: New Iran president a moderate who rallied extremes.
newsitem.headline: New Iran president a moderate who rallied extremes.

text.p: Mohammad Khatami, who has won the Iranian presidency by an astonishing landslide, is a moderate Islamic clergyman whose peculiar mixture of credentials enabled him to beat the odds and score the biggest political upset of Iran's 18-year revolution.
Conservative parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, the clerical establishment's candidate and pre-election favourite, on Saturday conceded defeat to Khatami, a former culture minister.

The 54-year-old Khatami's reputation as an open-minded Islamic intellectual and a tolerant politician gained him the support of a rainbow coalition ranging from Western-style liberals to radical Islamists, including some senior clerics.
He was widely backed by women, young people and intellectuals who feared a harder application of Islamic rules in everyday life and restrictions on freedom of expression.
His campaign was endorsed by centrists close to outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and Islamist left-wingers who have moderated many of their views in recent years.
This unlikely coalition was formed to counter conservatives accused by Khatami's supporters of trying to monopolise state power by adding the presidency to their control of parliament.
His moderate views have cost him in the past.

In 1992, Khatami was forced to resign after serving about 10 years as minister of culture and Islamic guidance under pressure from conservatives who attacked his relatively liberal policies which allowed cinema and books to flourish.
But his outspoken views, which include favouring more personal freedom, democracy and the rule of law, have been shielded by his religious credentials.

Born in Ardakan, a town on the edge of Iran's central desert, he is the son of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khatami, a respected cleric in the region, who joined the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's movement which deposed the Shah in 1979.
After the revolution, Khatami's father was appointed by Khomeini as the top clerical official in Ardakan, and later in the provincial capital of Yazd.
Khatami himself undertook Islamic studies in the Shi'ite religious learning centre of Qom where he also joined Khomeini's movement in the early 1960s.
He established close contacts with Khomeini's son Ahmad and together they were active in distributing Khomeini's books and other dissident Islamic material.

Khatami later received a university degree in philosophy and was appointed by senior clerics to head an Islamic centre in Hamburg, Germany, where he also perfected his German and English before the 1979 revolution.
A middle-ranking Shi'ite Moslem clergyman, he wears a black turban and has the title of Seyyed -- signs of a person believed to be a descendant of Islam's Prophet Mohammad.
Since his 1992 resignation, Khatami has stayed out of the political limelight, working as an adviser to Rafsanjani and heading Iran's national library.
His image as an outsider has helped Khatami appeal to Iranians at a time when his rival Nateq-Nouri was the candidate clearly identified with the conservative establishment.
But it remains to be seen if Khatami's credentials will enable him to work smoothly with powerful state bodies dominated by conservatives.

On the foreign policy front, Khatami is not expected to make radical changes to Iran's approach to the West, as Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has the final say on the key issues from foreign policy to the economy.
But Khatami has triggered controversy by suggesting that Iran could learn from the West and should not isolate itself.
Khatami is married and has two daughters and a son.
